analogy.p: Imagine trying to melt a huge block of rock-hard ice to free something frozen inside: it would take enormous energy. Adding a little salt lowers the melting point so the ice melts much more easily, just as cryolite lowers the melting point of aluminium oxide. The analogy breaks down because salt only lowers the freezing point of water, whereas cryolite actually dissolves the oxide and also helps the mixture conduct electricity.
analogy.t: A very sticky block of ice

bullets: **Electrolysis** is the breakdown of an ionic compound using electricity; the compound must be **molten or dissolved in water** so that its ions are free to move.
The ionic compound being broken down is **aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃**, which is purified from the ore **bauxite**.
Aluminium oxide is **dissolved in molten cryolite** to lower the operating temperature and save energy.
The products are **aluminium metal** (at the cathode) and **oxygen** (at the anode).
The **carbon anodes** react with the oxygen to make **carbon dioxide**, so the anodes wear away and must be replaced regularly.
Higher tier: write half equations such as **Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al** and **2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻**.
You may be asked to evaluate the process: it is very **energy hungry** (expensive) and releases **carbon dioxide**, but it produces a valuable, light, corrosion-resistant metal.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This spec point is about how **aluminium is manufactured** from its ore. You must be able to explain that aluminium is made by the **electrolysis of a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite**, say why cryolite is needed, describe what happens at each electrode, explain why the carbon anodes have to be replaced, and (at Higher tier) write balanced half equations. It sits inside the wider topic of electrolysis, and it is a favourite 6-mark "describe and explain" or "evaluate" question because it links reactivity, ionic bonding, energy use and environmental impact.

bullets: The reactivity series order to remember is: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, **aluminium**, (carbon), zinc, iron, copper.
A metal **above carbon** in the series cannot be reduced by carbon; a metal **below carbon** can.
**Reduction** is loss of oxygen (or gain of electrons); carbon can only remove oxygen from the oxides of less reactive metals.
Because aluminium forms very **strong ionic bonds** with oxygen, a lot of energy is needed to split the compound, which is why electricity is used.
Link to other topics: this is the same reasoning used for sodium, potassium and calcium, which are also made by electrolysis of molten compounds.
A common exam link: "Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis rather than by heating with carbon?" Answer: **aluminium is more reactive than carbon**.
Historically aluminium was a precious metal until electrolysis became practical, because the method needs large amounts of cheap electricity.
core.h: Why aluminium cannot be extracted by reduction with carbon
core.p: Metals found low in the reactivity series, such as iron and copper, can be extracted by **heating their oxides with carbon**, because carbon is more reactive than the metal and takes the oxygen away (a reduction). Aluminium is **more reactive than carbon**, so carbon cannot displace it from aluminium oxide. A different method is therefore needed, and electrolysis is the answer because electricity can force the metal ions to gain electrons even though they hold on to them very strongly.

bullets: Formula: **Al₂O₃**, made of **2 Al³⁺ ions for every 3 O²⁻ ions** so that the charges balance (+6 and −6).
Giant ionic lattice: strong forces between oppositely charged ions need **a lot of energy to overcome**, giving a very high melting point.
**Solid** aluminium oxide does not conduct because the ions are **in fixed positions** and cannot move.
**Molten** aluminium oxide conducts because the ions are **free to move** and carry the charge.
Bauxite is the **ore**: a rock containing enough of the compound to make extraction worthwhile.
Mining bauxite has environmental costs such as land use, habitat loss and waste material, which matter in evaluation answers.
The Higher tier idea that aluminium ions are 3+ and oxide ions are 2− comes from the groups: Al is in group 3 (loses 3 electrons), O is in group 6 (gains 2).
core.h: Aluminium oxide and its ore, bauxite
core.p: Aluminium is found in the Earth's crust combined with oxygen as **aluminium oxide**. The ore that is mined is **bauxite**, which is impure; the aluminium oxide is first purified before it goes into the electrolysis cell. Aluminium oxide is an **ionic compound** made of Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions held in a giant ionic lattice by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. This is why it has a **very high melting point** of roughly 2000 °C, and why it does not conduct electricity when solid.

bullets: The movement of **ions** completes the circuit inside the cell; the movement of **electrons** completes it in the wires.
**Positive ions** (Al³⁺) move to the **negative** cathode; **negative ions** (O²⁻) move to the **positive** anode (opposites attract).
An aluminium oxide solution in water is **not** used, because water would be electrolysed instead and hydrogen, not aluminium, would form at the cathode (aluminium is more reactive than hydrogen).
That is why a **molten** electrolyte is used for reactive metals such as aluminium, sodium and calcium.
Electrons are **supplied by the power supply** to the cathode and **removed from the anode**.
The electrodes must be **inert** (carbon/graphite conducts and does not dissolve), so that they do not take part in the reaction at the cathode.
The electrolyte is called the electrolyte because it is the liquid that **conducts and is broken down**.
core.h: Why the electrolyte must be molten
core.p: For electrolysis to work, the ionic compound must be a **liquid** (molten) or dissolved in water so that the ions can move to the electrodes. During electrolysis, positive ions (cations) are attracted to the negative electrode (the **cathode**) and negative ions (anions) are attracted to the positive electrode (the **anode**). Ions moving through the liquid are what carry the current inside the cell, while electrons carry the current in the wires.

bullets: Cryolite **lowers the melting point** of the mixture, so the cell runs at a much lower temperature than if pure Al₂O₃ were used.
Lower temperature means **less energy used for heating**, so lower costs and lower emissions from energy generation.
Cryolite does **not get used up** in the process; the aluminium oxide is what is split, and more oxide is added as it is consumed.
Model phrase for marks: "**cryolite is added to lower the melting point of the aluminium oxide, which saves energy / reduces cost**".
A weak answer says "cryolite is a catalyst" or "to make it react faster"; this is not what the mark scheme wants.
The numbers (about 2000 °C versus about 900 °C) are not usually needed, but the idea of **a big reduction** often earns the mark.
Link to other topics: dissolving in a molten solvent to lower a melting point is similar in idea to adding salt to ice to lower its freezing point.
core.p: Pure aluminium oxide melts at roughly **2000 °C**, so keeping it molten would need a huge amount of energy and very expensive equipment. To avoid this, the aluminium oxide is **dissolved in molten cryolite**, a compound of aluminium (sodium aluminium fluoride) which melts at a much lower temperature. The mixture is molten at roughly 900 to 1000 °C. This **lowers the melting point of the electrolyte**, which **saves energy and reduces cost**.

bullets: **Cathode (negative):** the carbon lining of the tank, where **aluminium ions gain electrons**.
**Anode (positive):** carbon blocks dipping into the electrolyte, where **oxide ions lose electrons**.
**Direct current (d.c.)** is used so that one electrode stays positive and one stays negative.
The electrolyte is **molten aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite**.
Liquid aluminium collects at the bottom because it is **denser than the electrolyte**; it is **tapped off** periodically.
A **very large current** is needed, so aluminium plants are often sited near sources of cheap electricity.
New aluminium oxide is **added continuously** as it is used up so that the process can keep running.
core.h: The electrolysis cell: apparatus and electrodes
core.p: The cell is a large steel tank lined with **carbon (graphite)**. The carbon lining is connected to the negative terminal and acts as the **cathode**. Large **carbon blocks (anodes)** are lowered into the molten mixture and are connected to the positive terminal. A very large direct current passes through the cell. The electrodes are carbon because carbon is a good conductor of electricity and is **unreactive towards the cryolite mixture**, although the anodes do react with oxygen as explained below.

bullets: Word equation idea: aluminium ions + electrons → aluminium.
Half equation (Higher tier): **Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al**.
Check charges: left side is +3 + (−3) = **0**, right side is 0, so the equation is balanced for charge.
This is **reduction** because the ion **gains electrons** (OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).
The metal produced is **molten aluminium**, collected as a layer at the bottom of the cell.
State symbols are not usually required, but Al is a liquid here because the cell is far above aluminium's melting point.
For every aluminium atom made, **3 electrons** are needed, which shows why so much electricity is used.
core.h: At the cathode: aluminium ions are reduced
core.p: Aluminium ions, **Al³⁺**, are positively charged so they move towards the negative cathode. Each ion **gains three electrons** and becomes a neutral aluminium atom. Gain of electrons is **reduction**. The aluminium produced is a liquid at the cell temperature, and because it is denser than the electrolyte it sinks to the bottom of the tank and can be tapped off.

bullets: Half equation (Higher tier): **2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻** (two oxide ions each lose 2 electrons, so 4 electrons in total).
Charge check: left side is 2 × (−2) = **−4**; right side is 4 × (−1) = **−4**, so the equation balances.
This is **oxidation** because oxide ions **lose electrons**.
The oxygen formed at the anode is a **diatomic molecule**: O₂, not just O.
Some oxygen reacts with the hot carbon anode: **C + O₂ → CO₂**, so carbon dioxide gas is released from the cell.
A balanced half equation must show **electrons** and the **correct charges**; marks are lost for unbalanced charge.
Link to other topics: the same idea explains why halide ions form halogens at the anode in the electrolysis of molten halides.
core.h: At the anode: oxide ions are oxidised
core.p: Oxide ions, **O²⁻**, are negatively charged so they move towards the positive anode. At the anode each oxide ion **loses two electrons**, and pairs of oxygen atoms bond to form **oxygen gas, O₂**. Loss of electrons is **oxidation**. The oxygen is formed at a very high temperature next to carbon, so it does not stay as oxygen for long.

bullets: Equation: **C + O₂ → CO₂**; the carbon of the anode is the reactant.
Anodes get **smaller and eventually stop working properly**, so they are changed on a regular basis.
Replacing anodes adds to the **cost** of making aluminium.
The CO₂ released contributes to **global warming** (a greenhouse gas).
The **cathode** (carbon lining) does not burn away because **no oxygen is produced there**.
Model phrase: "**the oxygen reacts with the carbon anodes to produce carbon dioxide, so the anodes burn away and need replacing**".
Common mistake: saying the anodes dissolve or are "used up by electrolysis"; the marks are for the reaction with oxygen.
core.h: Why the carbon anodes must be replaced
core.p: The oxygen produced at the anode is hot and reactive, and the anode is made of **carbon**. The oxygen **reacts with the carbon** to produce **carbon dioxide gas**. Because carbon is lost in this reaction, the anodes slowly **burn away and become smaller**, so they have to be **replaced regularly**. This is an extra cost of the process and a source of carbon dioxide emissions.

bullets: Overall: **2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂** (or in words: aluminium oxide → aluminium + oxygen).
Relative atomic masses: **Al = 27, O = 16**, so **Mr of Al₂O₃ = 2 × 27 + 3 × 16 = 102**.
Ratio from the equation: **2 mol Al₂O₃ (204 g) → 4 mol Al (108 g) + 3 mol O₂ (96 g)**; mass is conserved: 108 + 96 = 204.
Percentage of aluminium in the oxide = 54 ÷ 102 × 100 = **52.9%**, so a little over half of the mass of the oxide ends up as aluminium.
If the oxygen reacts with the anodes, the actual gas released is mostly **CO₂**, but the overall change at the electrodes still balances as above.
To scale up, always **divide by Mr to find moles**, use the **mole ratio**, then multiply by Ar: mass = moles × Ar.
Expect 2-mark and 3-mark calculation questions here at Higher tier; show each step clearly.
core.p: Combining the two electrode reactions gives the overall change: aluminium oxide is split into aluminium and oxygen. To balance the electrons, the cathode reaction is done four times (12 electrons) and the anode reaction three times (12 electrons). The result is **2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂**. Because this is a balanced chemical equation, you can use it with **relative formula masses** to work out the mass of aluminium that a given mass of oxide produces.

bullets: Molten aluminium layer: at the **bottom**, because it is **denser** than the molten mixture above it.
Tapping off the metal allows the process to run **continuously** without taking the cell apart.
Gas products rise out of the top of the cell and must be handled to **limit pollution**.
The **cryolite stays in the cell** and is reused (some is lost, which is another cost).
Pure aluminium made by electrolysis can then be cast, rolled or alloyed.
Link to other topics: the idea of collecting metal at the cathode and gas at the anode is the pattern for **all molten binary compounds**: metal at cathode, non-metal at anode.
Expect the question: "Why does the aluminium form at the bottom of the cell?" Answer: it is **a liquid and denser than the electrolyte**.
core.p: The two products are collected in different ways. The **aluminium is a liquid** at the temperature of the cell and, being **denser than the electrolyte**, it sinks to the bottom of the tank where it is **tapped off**. The **oxygen** is a gas, but it reacts with the hot carbon anodes to form **carbon dioxide**, which escapes from the cell. This is why the main gas released from an aluminium cell is carbon dioxide rather than oxygen.

bullets: **Energy cost:** a very large amount of **electricity** is needed (to melt the electrolyte and to supply the current), making it the main cost.
**Cryolite helps** by lowering the operating temperature, but the process is still energy intensive.
**Carbon dioxide** is released when the anodes burn away, and more CO₂ is produced if the electricity comes from fossil fuels.
**Anodes must be replaced regularly**, adding to cost.
**Mining bauxite** causes habitat destruction and waste, and the oxide has to be purified first.
**Benefit of recycling:** recycling aluminium needs far less energy than extracting it from ore, so it saves energy, money, ore and reduces landfill.
A good conclusion weighs benefits (useful, long-lasting, recyclable metal) against costs (energy, CO₂, mining) and says which is more important and why.
core.h: Evaluating the process: cost and environmental impact
core.p: Aluminium is a very useful metal: it has **low density**, resists **corrosion** because of a thin layer of aluminium oxide on its surface, and conducts electricity and heat. However, the process of extraction is **expensive** and has environmental effects. You need to give balanced points for a 6-mark evaluation, then reach a judgement.

bullets: Molten compound: **metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode** (e.g. lead bromide gives lead and bromine).
Aqueous solution of a reactive metal compound: **hydrogen** at the cathode because the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
Aluminium is above hydrogen in reactivity, which is why its oxide must be electrolysed **molten**, not in solution.
Aluminium oxide is **not soluble in water**, which also rules out an aqueous solution.
Inert electrodes (carbon/graphite) are used so they do not react with the products at the cathode.
In this unusual case the **anode does react** (with oxygen), unlike in most electrolysis questions where inert electrodes stay unchanged.
Link to topic **reactivity series**: the position relative to carbon and hydrogen decides the extraction method and the electrolysis product.
core.p: It helps to compare aluminium extraction with other electrolysis examples so that you can answer comparison questions and avoid mixing up products. In **molten** electrolysis of a binary ionic compound, the metal always forms at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode. In **aqueous** solutions, water also provides H⁺ and OH⁻ ions, so a more reactive metal such as aluminium would **not** be deposited; hydrogen would form instead.

bullets: Cathode: **Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al** (reduction, electrons on the left because they are gained).
Anode: **2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻** (oxidation, electrons on the right because they are lost).
Make electrons equal: lowest common multiple of 3 and 4 is **12**, so multiply cathode by **4** and anode by **3**.
**4Al³⁺ + 12e⁻ → 4Al** and **6O²⁻ → 3O₂ + 12e⁻**; add and cancel electrons: **4Al³⁺ + 6O²⁻ → 4Al + 3O₂**.
This is the same as **2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂**, because 2Al₂O₃ contains 4Al³⁺ and 6O²⁻.
Never write electrons as a product at the cathode: electrons are **reactants** there (gained).
Remember **OIL RIG**: Oxidation Is Loss (anode), Reduction Is Gain (cathode); the memory aid PANIC (Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode) also helps.
core.h: Higher tier: half equations in detail
core.p: At Higher tier you must write half equations that balance in both atoms and charge, and combine them. The method is: write the ion, decide whether it gains or loses electrons, add the electrons on the correct side so the **charges balance**, then check atoms. To combine the half equations, **multiply** them so that the numbers of electrons are equal, add them and cancel the electrons.

bullets: 1-mark: "Name the ore of aluminium" → **bauxite**; "Name the substance added" → **cryolite**.
2-mark: "Why is cryolite used?" → it **lowers the melting point** of aluminium oxide, which **saves energy / money**.
2-mark: "Why do the anodes need replacing?" → **oxygen reacts with carbon** to form **carbon dioxide**.
3-mark: "Describe what happens at the cathode" → Al³⁺ ions are **attracted to the cathode**, **gain electrons** (reduced) and form **aluminium** which sinks.
6-mark: structure answers in a logical chain as above, with a conclusion in an evaluation.
Always say **"molten"** and **"ions free to move"** when explaining why the electrolyte conducts.
Do not write "aluminium is extracted by smelting" or "reduced by carbon"; the method is **electrolysis**.
core.h: Common exam routes and linking ideas
core.p: Questions on this spec point appear as recall (1 or 2 marks), calculations (2 to 4 marks) and extended answers (6 marks). Always connect the **ideas in the right order**: reactivity (why electrolysis) → molten (ions free to move) → cryolite (lower melting point) → electrodes (carbon) → half equations → anode wear → products. Using this chain makes a 6-mark answer well organised and covers the mark scheme points.

exam: **State/name (1 mark):** bauxite is the ore, cryolite is the added substance, carbon (graphite) is the electrode material, aluminium forms at the cathode, oxygen at the anode.
**Explain why (2 marks):** give a point and a reason; e.g. "cryolite lowers the melting point (1), which saves energy/cost (1)".
**Why molten (2 marks):** "ions are free to move (1) so they can carry charge / reach the electrodes (1)"; solid ions are fixed in a lattice.
**Describe the electrode reactions (3 to 4 marks):** name the ion, say it moves to the oppositely charged electrode, say gain/loss of electrons, name the product.
**Anode replacement (2 marks):** "oxygen reacts with carbon (1) forming carbon dioxide, so the anode burns away (1)".
**Higher tier half equations:** check atoms **and** charges; electrons on the correct side; use the equations given in this note as models.
**Calculations:** write Mr first, then mole ratio from the balanced equation, then answer with units; show working to gain method marks.

**6-mark extended answer:** use a logical chain (reactivity, molten, cryolite, electrodes, half equations, products, anode wear) and include specific terms such as **ions, electrons, reduction, oxidation**.
**Evaluate (6 marks):** give at least two advantages and two disadvantages, then a clear **judgement** with a reason; mention recycling.
**Data questions:** compare melting points with and without cryolite using numbers and the idea of a lower energy requirement.

mistakes.r: Cryolite **lowers the melting point** of aluminium oxide so less energy is needed.
mistakes.w: Cryolite is a catalyst, or makes the reaction faster.

mistakes.r: Aluminium is **more reactive than carbon**, so it must be extracted by **electrolysis**.
mistakes.w: Aluminium is extracted by heating with carbon.

mistakes.r: **Oxygen reacts with the carbon anodes** forming carbon dioxide, so they burn away.
mistakes.w: The anodes dissolve or are used up.

mistakes.r: Electrons are **gained** at the cathode, so they appear on the **left**: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al.
mistakes.w: Writing the cathode reaction as Al³⁺ → Al + 3e⁻.

mistakes.r: Oxygen is a molecule, **O₂**, formed from O²⁻ losing electrons: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻.
mistakes.w: Oxygen is formed as O or written as O⁻.

mistakes.r: **Electrons** move in the wires; **ions** move through the electrolyte.
mistakes.w: The ions move through the wires.

mistakes.r: It is **molten** (dissolved in molten cryolite); in water, hydrogen would form instead.
mistakes.w: Aluminium oxide is dissolved in water for electrolysis.

mistakes.r: Molten aluminium is **denser** than the electrolyte so it **sinks** and is tapped off from the bottom.
mistakes.w: The aluminium is lighter so it floats at the top.

summary: You must explain how aluminium is manufactured by electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite, describe what happens at the carbon electrodes (including why the anodes are replaced), write half equations at Higher tier and evaluate the cost and environmental impact. It matters because it combines reactivity, ionic bonding, energy and sustainability in one commonly examined process.

terms.d: The breakdown of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by an electric current.
The molten or dissolved ionic compound that is broken down during electrolysis.
The negative electrode, to which positive ions move; reduction happens here.
The positive electrode, to which negative ions move; oxidation happens here.
A compound of aluminium (sodium aluminium fluoride) in which aluminium oxide is dissolved to lower its melting point.
The main ore of aluminium, containing aluminium oxide.
A rock containing enough metal or metal compound to make it economic to extract the metal.
A charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.
Gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen).
Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen).
An equation showing the change at one electrode, including electrons, balanced for atoms and charge.
An electrode that does not react with the electrolyte or products, such as graphite or platinum.
Melted into a liquid state; ions can move freely.
A list of metals in order of how readily they react; it decides the method of extraction.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the formula shown.

worked.ans: 270 kg of aluminium (and the other 240 kg of the 510 kg is oxygen; 270 + 240 = 510).
worked.q: Aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) is electrolysed. Calculate the mass of aluminium produced from 510 kg of aluminium oxide. Relative atomic masses: Al = 27, O = 16. (3 marks)
steps: Moles of Al₂O₃ = 510 000 g ÷ 102 = 5000 mol (or 5 kmol).
Mole ratio Al₂O₃ : Al = 2 : 4 = 1 : 2, so moles of Al = 5000 × 2 = 10 000 mol.

worked.q: Write half equations for the reactions at the cathode and anode, and combine them to give the overall equation. (4 marks, Higher tier)
steps: Make the electrons equal: lowest common multiple is 12, so ×4 for the cathode and ×3 for the anode.
Add them and cancel 12e⁻ on each side: 4Al³⁺ + 6O²⁻ → 4Al + 3O₂.
This is 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂ because 2Al₂O₃ contains 4 Al³⁺ and 6 O²⁻.

worked.ans: Model answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon so electrolysis is used. Aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the melting point and save energy. In the molten mixture the ions are free to move. Al³⁺ ions are attracted to the negative electrode where they gain electrons (Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al) and aluminium collects at the bottom. O²⁻ ions are attracted to the positive carbon electrodes where they lose electrons (2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻). The oxygen reacts with the carbon anodes to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes must be replaced.
worked.q: Describe and explain how aluminium is extracted from aluminium oxide. (6 marks)
steps: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so it cannot be extracted by reduction with carbon; electrolysis is used.
The aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower its melting point, which saves energy and reduces cost.
The mixture is molten so the ions (Al³⁺ and O²⁻) are free to move.
Aluminium ions move to the negative carbon cathode, gain three electrons (reduction) and form molten aluminium, which sinks and is tapped off.
Oxide ions move to the positive carbon anode, lose electrons (oxidation) and form oxygen.
The oxygen reacts with the carbon anodes to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes burn away and have to be replaced.
